chapter_theme: The deluge (பிரளயம்): when the flood covers the world and the gods contend, Siva alone stands as light and mountain above the waters, tells the gods not to fear, and keeps the sea within bounds; the gods praise him without knowing his purpose.

362.reading: When the flood rose and covered the dark mountains and the two contended, each crying 'I am king', the Lord alone became a towering light reaching down into the water and stood as a mountain no one could scale, and gave grace.
362.nuance: இருவர் (the two) are traditionally Brahma and Vishnu, and கோ (king) their claim to supremacy; the verse folds the column of fire story, told fully in chapter 41, into the deluge. ஒருவனும் stresses that he alone stands.

363.reading: The one who bears the name Lord of the gods of the universe cut through the surging sea and, seeing the world in its fire, ran without falling in and said 'Fear not' so that they would not fall into the mouth of the waves.
363.nuance: உலகார் அழற்கண்டு may be 'seeing the fire that fills the world' or 'seeing the world's people in distress'. அஞ்சல் (fear not) is the gesture of protection, and the verse's centre.

364.reading: The immortals and gods whom the cool sea let go bow to him as our Lord encircled by the eight seas, but they do not know the purpose of the one who rises above the sky-sea and beyond it.
364.nuance: விண்கடல் (sky-sea) and கண்கடல் செய்யும் (makes a sea of the eye, or makes the sea vast) are obscure. The plain point is the gap between worship and knowing: the gods praise him and still don't grasp his intent.

365.reading: Who in this world can order things as he does, the one praised as self-born and able to create? When the roar of the sea swelled over the bewildering waters, he set a fire within it so that it would not overflow.
365.nuance: The fire set in the sea is traditionally the submarine mare's-head fire (வடவைத்தீ) that drinks the ocean and keeps it from flooding the land. The verse names only அங்கி (fire). சயம்பு (svayambhu) is often an epithet of Brahma, so the first line may contrast praise of Brahma with Siva's real ordering power.

366.reading: Going beyond the worship that ruins good qualities, he sought out the friend seated in the lotus whose eye does not fail, took that head, and took up a way of living that heaven does not blame.
366.nuance: The verse plays on பழி (blame, ruin) in every line. அச்சிரம் (that head) and the one in the lotus point to the story of Siva taking Brahma's fifth head and then going about begging with the skull; that is tradition's reading, and the verse's own sense is obscure. Its link to the deluge is not clear.

links.note: 362 mentions in passing the two who quarrel over who is king while the Lord stands as light; 372 tells the same quarrel as the search for the head and feet of the column of fire, naming Brahma and Vishnu and their folly.
Both turn on Siva carrying a skull: 366, as tradition reads it, the head he took from Brahma; 371 the bones and skulls of the gods he bears so they won't crumble to dust.

source_issues: 364 line 4 (கண்கடல் செய்யும்) and 366 as a whole are obscure; the sense may be corrupt or depend on lost context.
